Mr. Speaker, last night the Glengarry, Prescott and Russell Federations of Agriculture met in my constituency to express their dissatisfaction and frustration with the federal Tory Government, and more particularly with the Finance Minister's Budget. Whereas Mr. Brian Mulroney during the last election campaign made a written promise to provide agriculture with long-term financing at stable and affordable rates, and
Whereas farm financing was not addressed in the recent Budget,

subsubtopic: STOCKHOLM MEETING OF SOCIAL DEMOCRATIC PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week in Stockholm, Social Democratic Parties from around the globe met to consider joint action to deal with the grim economic crisis in the world. The Members of the Socialist International endorsed a report from their economic policy committee stressing three broad conclusions.
The first of these conclusions is that, to spur world economic recovery, the industrialized countries must reject the prevailing approach of fiscal cut-backs and high interest rates, and plan a joint strategy of expansionary public expenditures focused on community needs. Second, the dangerous debt
crisis of the developing countries must be tackled with what amounts to a redistribution of purchasing power to poorer countries to help revive world economic demand. Third, solutions to the debt crisis will require an international conference to forgive debts for the very poorest countries, reduce interest payments for others, and tie repayments to export earning levels in the Third World. I cal! on the Canadian Government to provide leadership in such international action to respond to this debt crisis.

Mr. Speaker, the preservation and creation of jobs are uppermost in the minds of all Members of this House. The shipbuilding and repairing industry has a ready-made capacity to create jobs now. The most efficient Canadian yards are using modern technology and advanced systems of management.
Governments in other countries have traditionally supported their shipyards in ways which make free competition virtually impossible. Previously, through subsidies and grants, Canada supported the shipbuilding industry in an amount approximating $4,000 per employee per year. Yards were busy. Today Canadian yards are struggling to survive.
Work is going on offshore at the expense of Canadian workmen. Welfare rates for a single unemployed person amount to over $4,000 per year. Unemployment insurance payments come to another $13,000 annually. Support, therefore, for the shipbuilding industry would achieve a net gain for every additional job created. Those workmen would then be paying income tax and contributing to social welfare programs, instead of drawing upon them.
A buoyant shipbuilding industry would be the shot in the arm needed by our steel industry, and would have numerous spin-off economic benefits. The shipping industry in a country such as ours, with its miles of coastline and an inland waterway comparable to none other in the world deserves the support of a Government such as this which has always put its priority on jobs, jobs, jobs. It deserves more.

June 21, 1985

subsubtopic: LAC LA HACHE INDIAN BAND-EFFECT OF URANIUM MINING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last few days Indian people from the Lac la Hache Indian Band, and environmentalists, have blockaded the road to the uranium mine at Wollaston Lake operated by Eldorado Nuclear Ltd.
The uranium deposits at Wollaston Lake are among the largest and richest in the world, and Eldorado Nuclear plans to keep mining there for at least 20 years. Then Eldorado will leave, but it will not take its garbage with it. Indian people will have to live with radioactive pollution for generations and generations.
Indian people take very seriously not only their aboriginal rights but also their aboriginal responsibilities to take care of the land for future generations.
When a 76-year-old elder toured the mine and saw what was happening, he said:
I almost cried when I saw what they have done to the land. If I would have known I would never have let this happen to my trap line. They didn't tell me all the problems uranium makes. I didn't know the mining would pollute the water, or that uranium is used in nuclear bombs. The mining companies should not be here. This is Indian land.
As inhabitants of planet Earth, we desperately need to realize that the struggle of the Lac la Hache Indians is also our struggle. We too have a responsibility to preserve the earth for future generations. The mining and the pollution must stop.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Government provided the Opposition lets us to do so quickly, will authorize payment of $285 million in lump sum supplementary fiscal equalization payments to the six provinces that are receiving equalization payments. This is in addition to some $5 billion the provinces will be receiving annually under the fiscal equalization program.
In making this announcement, our admirable Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stated, and I quote:
These payments are substantial and should be of considerable assistance to the poorer provinces in meeting their commitments, especially with respect to essential services.
The Minister of Finance also mentioned that these amounts were the most the Government was able to afford in this respect, in light of its own serious financial situation, something the provinces can appreciate.
The decision follows consultations held with the provinces in recent months. It takes into account the concerns of the provinces about the level of equalization payments resulting in some cases from the expiry of the special transitional guarantee introduced in 1982 by the former Government, and which has brought about a significant decline in federal transfer payments, especially for Quebec and Manitoba. Our most

Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments admirable Minister of Finance will soon be reviewing the equalization program with the provinces, in connection with the general review of fiscal arrangements between now and March 31, 1987.
Generally, the equalization formula is based on the population of a province and on its capacity to raise revenues, so that payments vary from province to province. The Minister of Finance has stated that the Government will make these supplementary lump sum payments which in fact it did not have to make under the present fiscal arrangements, in its concern to be fair and equitable to the provinces, at a time when financial restrictions are the order of the day at all levels of government. The Minister noted that over-all Federal transfers to the provinces, within the framework of equalization and established programs financing, are estimated to rise from $19.7 billion for the past fiscal year to $20.7 billion for fiscal 1985-86. For 1984-85, equalization payments would total $5,403 billion.
Mr. Speaker, the Bill will eliminate the shortcomings in a formula which is no longer readily applicable as a result of changing trends in the economic situation since it was first implemented.
The provinces have been made aware of the situation, of course, and some of them were not in complete agreement. Other provinces endorsed the measure since they considered that we had established a program which took their concerns into account.
The most significant consideration at this third reading stage is that the provinces are waiting for their payments. The Government is prepared to make those payments should the House co-operate and give speedy approval to the Bill. Since we do have a number of Bills to study and pass before the House adjourns next week, I seek the co-operation of all Hon. Members. I should think that everything has been said about this issue, so I urge all Parties in the House to show goodwill and adopt this Bill as soon as possible.

speechtext:
In response to the invitation of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier), Mr. Speaker, I am quite prepared to co-operate on behalf of the Party I represent. But there are still some disturbing facts which, in 1986-87 and even in 1985-86, will put some provinces in a difficult situation. We are now at the third reading of Bill C-39, the Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments (1982-87) Act.
Mr. Speaker, I must point out that no amendment has been made to this Bill even though the Opposition did make strong representations. We came up with particularly convincing arguments during the second reading debate and before the committee, and the Minister of Finance of Quebec had made serious representations of his own. In these circumstances, the arguments I made last April 18 are still valid, mutatis mutan-di, in the sense that although this measure does provide
equalization payments for certain provinces, as it is drafted it falls far short in the case of the Province of Nova Scotia.
It is unfair as well to the Province of Manitoba and, as far as Quebec is concerned, I think that the qualifier I used last April has lost none of its appropriateness-this Bill is inequitable.
The Parliamentary Secretary mentioned the interim payments formula. Hon. Members will recall that the interim payments formula had been included in the 1982-87 fiscal arrangements as a kind of guarantee to the provinces in case the new formula that had been adopted did not produce results.
It was obvious, that whatever happened, the Government in power from 1985-86 would have to review this formula since the results were positive in some provinces and negative in others. It would therefore be necessary to amend the guarantee formula so that the provinces would not have to come back once more in 1986-87 to wait in line before the Office of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) or the Office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to try to obtain a more equitable treatment.
Mr. Speaker, the Province of Nova Scotia, for example, received $620 million in 1984-85 in equalization payments. This includes the $72 million which Nova Scotia received in transition payments. As of 1985-86 these transition payments will no longer exist. Bill C-39 offers only temporary compensation to the Province of Nova Scotia. The compensation will only apply in the fiscal year of 1985-86. The federal Government has announced that it will renegotiate fiscal arrangements with the provinces by March 31, 1987. This means that no provision has been made for Nova Scotia for the fiscal year 1986-87. Nova Scotia is left at the mercy of the federal Government and will have to count on a special lobbying effort in order to defend its own interests.
The fact that Nova Scotia must now rely on political lobbying is particularly unfortunate. Equalization was established precisely to avoid the need for poorer provinces to come begging on a discretionary basis to the federal Government.
I am sad that the Conservative Government is politicizing the principle of equalization. This is particularly unfortunate for Nova Scotia at this time because it is highly unlikely that the Government will undertake the very political energy talks without consideration to the equalization negotiations. Equalization is in danger of being used as a carrot, or a stick, rather than as an instrument of national unity.
The financial and economic agenda of Nova Scotia has not yet been addressed. The Budget heralds a new era for the Canadian energy industry. Next year's financial and economic situation of Nova Scotia is still up in the air.
Bill C-39 is also unfair to the Province of Manitoba. Under the new equalization formula Manitoba received $439 million

in 1982-83, which included $169 million in transition payments. In 1983-84, Manitoba received $466 million, of which $163 million were transition payments. In 1984-85, the province received $479 million, of which $138 million as in transition payments. In general, Manitoba received 30 per cent of its equalization thanks to these transition payments.
Now that the transition program will be ending, the equalization payment to Manitoba will decline from $479 million to $407 million. This is a reduction of $72 million. Despite the fact that this Bill will provide some compensation for this current fiscal year, equalization payments to Manitoba will be reduced substantially in the fiscal year 1986-87.

As for Quebec, the formula proposed by the Minister of Finance in Bill C-39 is completely inequitable. Because the Government of Canada did not want to maintain, for the last two years of the fiscal arrangements, the transitional guarantee provisions which had been in effect during the last three years of these arrangements, the Province of Quebec will incur very substantial losses. For instance, after receiving $3.7 billion in 1984-85, Quebec will get only $2.7 billion in 1985-86, which means a loss of $290 million. In 1986-87, it is forecast that the equalization payments received by Quebec will amount to $2.9 billion, or $172 million less that in 1984-85.
If we consider the normal growth in equalization payments which should be generated from one year to the next, the loss for Quebec is substantial, and Bill C-39 only makes up 15 per cent of the equalization losses suffered by Quebec because the transitional guarantee provisions no longer apply.
During the debates on this issue, the Quebec Finance Minister had clearly indicated how the decision of the Conservative Government would affect the cash flow of the Quebec Treasury. Following the comments made by the Quebec Finance Minister, the Prime Minister of Canada said that the door was still open and that further negotiations could take place. For all practical purposes, he suggested that there would be some improvement, but as usual, this was only a smokescreen, statements for the press which had no concrete results since the Bill has come back to us in the same form.
To my knowledge, there were no further intense negotiations with Quebec, but it is quite clear and obvious that the Government of Canada did not change its approach and that Quebec will lose hundreds of millions of dollars in 1985-86 and 1986-87, which will result eventually in a heavier tax burden for Quebec residents.
When we considered Bill C-39 at the second reading and committee stages, the Budget had not yet been brought down. However, Mr. Speaker, according to the indications given by the Minister of Finance of Canada last May 23, provincial transfer payments will have decreased by $2 billion in 199091. This means that Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Quebec will be affected not only during the next two years under the present Fiscal arrangements, but also that they must expect
Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments other cutbacks beginning in 1986-87. The same will be true for all the provinces who receive equalization payments and transfers.
I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that those two measures, the one introduced in Bill C-39 and the announcement made in the budget, raise Financing problems for our Confederation as a whole.
Unless the Canadian Government is ready once again to renege on its election promises and jeopardize the universality of social programs, I do not see, once the Conservative Government has slashed $2 billion from its payments to the provinces, how the latter will manage to administer the post-secondary education programs, health care, medicare, and the Canadian Assistance Plan without increasing their own taxes, or imposing user fees which the Progressive Conservative Party fought when they were the Opposition.
Let us not hide our heads in the sand. The message set out in Bill C-39, and driven home by the Budget, is telling Canadians the Conservative Government is getting ready to renege on another of its election promises, even though in December 1984 the debate on the universality of social programs seemed quite clear.
This Conservative Government is sending out the message that it will try and do indirectly what it would not do directly last December.
Successive Liberal Governments have developed over the years a series of programs aimed at strengthening Canadian unity with a balance of services offered to all citizens of Canada, in whatever village, town, city, region or province they lived.
Those programs brought in a whole concept of funding for this confederation of ours, a concept which is jeopardized not only by Bill C-39 but by the message the Minister of Finance delivered to this House and the Canadian people on May 23, 1985.
I do not believe Canadians are ready to accept such a change without a substantive debate amongst the Canadian people and the Governments that operate those programs, whether provincial or federal. I do not believe that Canadians are willing to see their medical care, hospital care, and postsecondary education programs slashed, but they are not willing either to shoulder the Fiscal burden of those programs that have been contracted between the national Government and the provincial Governments, either to have the axe fall on those programs or to alter the funding and transfer the full fiscal burden of the administration of such programs from the federal Government to the provincial Governments.
This is why the Official Opposition will not support this Bill on third reading, because it is inadequate and because it is not fair to the provinces of Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Quebec, not only for fiscal year 1985-86 but also for fiscal year 1986-87.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to be fairly brief in speaking to this matter.
First, I want to commend my friend, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) for his very careful analysis of the present situation and thoughtful review of what might well be the consequences of what essentially is a stopgap measure. We cannot provide adequate financing to the provinces in this way and expect them to be able to do any long-term planning.
Quite clearly, the intent of the equalization payment program was to allow provinces to be able to plan for their health care needs, educational needs and housing needs to an extent with some degree of assuredness. Therefore, they would need to know what kind of equalization would be available on a long-term formula basis so they could anticipate what financing would be coming from the federal Government. My friend from the Liberal Party has set that out well.
When there are gaps in the federal Government's commitment to ongoing finance, it causes concern because the provinces are left in a position of subservience in making representations on an annual basis to the federal Government. They must try to accommodate the federal Government's desire to establish new budgetary provisions. It will be very difficult for at least two of the provinces most directly affected to anticipate their revenues for the fiscal year 1987.
I would be remiss if I did not point out the battle that was fought by all provinces, particularly the Province of Manitoba initially, to confront the federal Government when it became apparent that the payments that had been proposed were woefully inadequate. I think it is fair to say that some degree of recognition should be paid to that province's Government, as it must to all Governments of the provinces, that they managed to exert the pressure that brought us to this point today.
Let me repeat the intent of the equalization system because, as the name implies, it is a way to try to provide a share of the substantial wealth that is generated in the balance of the country to those provinces which do not have the same economic capacity. The purpose of this plan is to assure the citizens who live in those less advantaged areas of an opportunity to enjoy an adequate level of public service for themselves and their children. It will enable those who live in the less economically fortunate areas of the country to have a standard of education that will enable their children to have the same employment opportunities in any part of the country and to participate in the ongoing events of Canada.
When we tamper with equalization payments, it is not simply a Government to Government arrangement. It involves people, a commitment from people who live in the more fortunate areas of the country to share with the people who live in the less economically fortunate parts of this country. In this way, growth will take place from coast to coast.
I want to caution the Government that in the case of Nova Scotia, as with Manitoba and probably Quebec, there will be problems in two years unless a new regime is put into place before 1987. Negotiations must be completed and a long-term proposal for equalization that is acceptable across the country put in place before we reach that period of uncertainty when it may once again be necessary to lobby the Government to become the main instrument to achieve fairness.
The fact is that this Bill must be viewed as a stopgap, and therefore inadequate. However, it is with that in mind that we accept the commitment of the Government at this point that it is prepared to move to negotiate an arrangement that will ultimately result in a fair distribution of wealth, which will ultimately provide the maintenance and advancement of many programs provided in those areas that are so dependent on equalization payments to sustain their economy.
I believe that there will be a much more intense debate on this subject in a year and a half to two years from now. I anticipate that debate to be centered on what will take place as we enter the 1990s. It will primarily reflect the intransigence that the Government has displayed in recognizing the necessity for the maintenance of the social system in Canada. If the Government takes the same approach to equalization as it has with respect to the financing of social policy and reneges on its commitment to fair and equitable economic growth through equalization, we will see a battle being fought not unlike the battle presently being waged against the deindexation of pensions.

speechtext:
I am going to say a few words regardless of any deals that have been made behind the scenes because we are talking about a very important subject. We are talking about equalization payments. We are talking about equalization payments that are supposed to equalize opportunity across the nation to provincial Governments for the amounts of money needed in order to get an equalization of services across the country. In other words, what the provinces cannot make up for in their normal tax revenues, what they cannot raise locally within a province to make up the average amount necessary, is given to them as an equalization payment every year. In other words, the rich give to the poor. The federal Government, through this mechanism, is supposed to go a long way in trying to give the poor provinces of Canada adequate funds to allow them to have some semblance of services. Regardless of whether you live in Newfoundland, Alberta or Manitoba, at least the services given to the people should be approximately the same.
The Parliamentary Secretary, in introducing this Bill, condemned the former Liberal administration and said there had been cuts.
I would like to remind the Parliamentary Secretary, as far as this Bill is concerned, of what is contained in the Budget in one sentence on page 18, which reads:
To spread the burden of expenditure reduction fairly, the Government will also be seeking to limit the rate of growth of transfers to provinces to yield annual savings of $2 billion by the end of the decade.
It says, "To yield annual savings of $2 billion by the end of the decade." It goes on:
In 1990-91, they would represent about the same share of total program expenditures as they do today.
In other words, there would be an extreme limitation from what the former bad, terrible Liberal Government had in place. This Government in the Budget it had just presented is going to have annual savings of $2 billion by the end of the decade. That sets it in focus. If the Liberals reduced equalization payments, then there is now going to be a further substantial reduction in the rate of increase.
If you look at the services provided across this country that are supposed to be subsidized through the equalization formula so that they will be approximately equal, you will see a great diversity of them. You could go to the richest province, some people claim that that is Alberta, and you would see assistance in the form of workmen's compensation that is not as good as that which you would see in Newfoundland. There is a great divergence. You would see less of a minimum wage in Alberta than you have in Newfoundland. You would see great differences in the services given to the general public.
It must be borne in mind that a lot of the measures serving the public are the decisions of the provincial administrations. When you get into the payment of welfare, of social services, you see a great difference. Sometimes you see the poorer provinces receiving equalization payments giving better services than some of the richer provinces.
If you get hurt in Alberta and you have to go on workman's compensation and then you go back home to Newfoundland to live, you discover that your payment is less than if you had
Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments
been hurt in Newfoundland and were still living in Newfoundland. If you were working in Newfoundland at minimum wage, you would find it higher than the minimum wage paid in Alberta. By the same token, if you were in any other province in Canada you could have some services in daycare centres, the cost shared by the federal Government, but in Newfoundland you would not have that same service. That is a decision of the provincial administration.
Where you really see the difference in services to the general public, Mr. Speaker, is in the area of infrastructure. A provincial government Department tries to do certain things. If its responsibility is in transportation, it would try to upgrade and pave roads. If its area is municipal affairs, water and sewer services, the Department would try to improve that. Where do they get the money from? If you looked at provincial Governments, in the poor provinces you would see that half of the money given, if you took the percentage, comes from the federal Government in equalization payment. That is the purpose of the equalization payment, to have an equality of services even in infrastructure.
The Newfoundland Government, the Nova Scotia Government or the New Brunswick Government could not pave the number of roads they are paving or what they are doing without these equalization payments. It boils down to what their priorities are. It boils down to what happens in their Cabinet meetings and what happens to the equalization money, because it represents a blank cheque, Mr. Speaker.
Transfer payments over the years have become blank cheques. It was not too long ago that you made a payment according to a percentage of what a provincial Government spent, say, on senior citizens' homes or nursing homes. Then we changed it to block funding, so provinces got the funding which increased as a percentage every year. It was given with no strings attached. The provincial Government could decide what it was going to do with the federal money. We saw provincial Governments throughout Canada putting a freeze on building senior citizens homes but still receiving the money and the increase and then redirecting it in different directions.
When you talk, as the new Budget does, about reducing these transfer payments to $2 billion annually, you are not really giving the provincial Governments a chance to do what they are supposed to do and I am not saying they are doing what they are supposed to do because they are not.
Take a look at some of the so-called poor provinces, Mr. Speaker. There are people in Canada today in 1985 who do not have community water systems, yet there is supposed to be equalization under the equalization formula. People in some communities are drinking contaminated water out of an existing system or from wells that pick up surface water from the highway. When you realize that that is the case today in 1985 in a great many ridings represented by MPs in this Chamber, you have to say that something is wrong. Somebody's priorities are wrong. It just so happens that it is the priorities of the provincial Governments that are wrong. No matter how much money is given to the provinces in equalization payments, they have formulas for supplying services to the general public.

June 21, 1985
Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments
Perhaps there should be even more strings attached to equalization payments.
People in Ottawa and in other major centres across Canada think nothing of turning on taps and drinking tap water. It is a normal occurrence. They do not think about it until they visit communities such as some in my riding of Gander-Twillingate and discover that they cannot turn on taps because they do not exist, or when they turn on taps that the water is not drinkable.
When we look at equalization of services across the country, at equalization formulas and at the Act, they look great. It sounds good to equalize payments across Canada and to equalize services to the general public. However, when we look at some of the smaller communities in the country, we discover that they have no drinking water. In 1985, in this great country of Canada, there are schools with no drinking water and there are wells which contain contaminated water. We have to wonder about equalization in services when we drive down unpaved roads in some communities and there is dust everywhere. The women in those communities will tell us that they cannot hang out their clothes or that it is difficult to paint their houses because of the dust. We must remember the actual rationale behind equalization payments.
No matter what is the decision of a provincial administration, whether it is good or bad, whether it tries to save money when it should not be trying to save money, and regardless of how it treats the poorest within its provincial jurisdiction, the federal Government cannot say that it will try to save $2 billion annually under the equalization formula. In the meantime, it introduces a Bill in the House and kicks in $200 million to make it look good. However, in reality, it is cutting back $2 billion annually from the equalization formula.
When we look at the services to the general public and at what Members of Parliament have to deal with every day, we see some incredible differences in provincial legislation dealing with payments to individuals. For example, we find that some provinces have 90-day rules respecting welfare or social assistance. When individuals attend welfare offices, they are asked what amount of money they made in the last 90 days. If a person has made more than he would receive on welfare, he has to wait until it runs out. In the meantime, what is he supposed to do if he has children attending school and has to pay perhaps as much as $100 per child for school books? He has to live, but he is faced with the 90-day rule. We must remember that the Government of the province in which he lives is obtaining half its budget from the federal Government in equalization payments. The rules indicate that there must be an equalization of opportunity in Canada, but we see, for example, a Tory Government in the Province of Newfoundland with the audacity to turn around and make the 90-day rule.
Other provinces will tell welfare recipients who are living with people over 18 years of age that they cannot obtain anything from welfare. What does this mean to a woman on widow's allowance with three children over the age of 18 years living at home, who cannot find work, and is not receiving
payments from a provincial Government which is receiving massive equalization payments from the federal Government? However, if she moves to Ontario or to some other province, she discovers that the system is completely different.
I could point to things like minimum wages and workmen's compensation. They are much better in Newfoundland than they are in Alberta, Saskatchewan or British Columbia. They are equal to those in Ontario, but they are not better than those in Manitoba or in Quebec. In fact, Quebec has one of the best minimum wage schemes in Canada.
My point is that regardless of what provincial Governments do with their money, regardless of how bad they are-and just by accident, they are Tory Governments and there is no equalization in services to the general public across the country-we cannot have a federal Government which is prepared to cut back even further or will not even give provincial administrations a chance. The new federal Government is saying that it will cut back by $2 billion annually to provincial administrations.
It is all right for the Government to introduce this Bill which provides a momentary increase, a drop in the bucket, a smidgen of hope, but we must keep in mind what it did after it introduced this Bill-it slashed by $2 billion annually.

Mr. Speaker ... do sit down my friend!
Mr. Speaker, we are about to complete our study of Bill C-24, a legislation providing for the termination of the Canadian Home Insulation and Canadian Oil Substitution programs.
Hon. Members from both sides of the House will agree, I am sure, that this bill has been fully considered. On more than 90 occasions, comments were made during debate on second reading.
The closer we look, the more we realize that the current state of the economy compels us, as the Government, to speed up the rationalization process of the budgetary spending under various programs, including the Canadian Oil Substitution Program and the Canadian Home Insulation Program.
Our Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works has held most constructive hearings and heard testimonies from such organizations as the Canadian Gas Association and the National Association of Insulation and Energy Conservation Contractors. There seems to be general support for the government's decision to phase out these programs.
The years during which the need for these programs was the greatest are long gone, a fact that is well recognized both by the public and the industry. And I dare hope, Mr. Speaker, that it is also acknowledged by Members opposite.
Since it is necessary indeed, essential, to reduce the national debt, it would therefore be utopian at this stage to try to lessen the deficit burden while advocating a welfare state.
Thus, Bill C-24 represents the will of this government to strive even more to stabilize its spending and balance its budget as any conscientious administrator should do. Moreover, it should be kept in mind that the decision to bring to an end sooner the COSP and CHIP programs is also due to the fact that conditions have greatly changed since their inception. Our government recognizes, Mr. Speaker, that since the Canadian market place has undergone a change, the state's role in the substitution of oil and the conservation of energy must also change.
The CHIP program has created a market for home insulation products and has led to the sitting up of a specialized installation industry throughout the country. Moreover, the CHIP program has succeeded in making owners aware of the importance of energy conservation and of the benefits of insulation in terms of greater comfort and lower heating bills.
Mr. Speaker, it is of the utmost importance for all Canadians to understand that future conservation depends on present investments. Some 2.8 million Canadian homes have received financial aid and before the program is terminated, over $1 billion will have been spent. Substantial energy savings have
Oil Substitution Act
been made and the over-all assessment of the program shows that such expenditures have proved worthwhile.
The COSP program has shown that since 1980, significant savings have been made in terms of heating costs through the conversion from oil to natural gas, electricity or wood. The program has promoted the development and marketing of high performance systems, for example, slow-combustion gas heaters, electric heat pumps and controlled combustion stoves.
The COSP and CHIP programs have made it possible to conserve some 75,000 barrels of oil per day or its equivalent in other energy forms.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, this is an outstanding achievement in the management of our energy ressources. Further progress must be made with regard to oil substitution, the upgrading of heating systems and energy performance of existing houses, and this, by reinsulating them and making them airtight. Such progress will require different environment and energy markets than those existing when the COSP and CHIP programs were implemented.

What does it offer in return? It offers studies, proposals, and a promise to look at the impact of its actions. It is a Government that lives on hindsight. It does not care about the future.
This Bill ends the hope of energy security in the country. The Government says that it is okay to cut off incentives for consumers, because Canadians are energy conscious now. That is far from the truth. This week, the International Energy Agency said that Canada was one of the most inefficient users of energy resources in the western world. What did the Government do? It cut off the incentives which helped Canadians to conserve energy and save on their energy costs.
The report of the International Energy Agency was very interesting. It said that Canadian energy efficiency started out at the same level as the United States ten years ago, but has become an energy waster since that time. The International Energy Agency is a very reputable organization. It has criticized the Government for ending the Canadian Oil Substitution Program and for phasing out the Canadian Home Insulation Program. In fact, the report predicts that under the

The Government is gambling with our energy future. It is becoming complacent. It says that we have enough oil and gas. It says that we do not have to worry about the future. That is wrong. That is the attitude which the report warns against. The International Energy Agency forecasts a tight oil market by the end of the century with an "increasing risk of massive upward price movements in the event of any disruption of supplies". Yet, the Government is cutting off the incentive to conserve energy, not only with this Bill, but with the many other worth-while energy conservation programs which have been cut.
The Canada Energy Audit Program will be ended. That program featured 10 specially-designed energy buses which provided special mobile energy audit services throughout Canada. That is another program for Canadian consumers which has been cut.
The Government has ended the Atlantic Canada Capital Investment Program. It is hard to believe that it could find more things to cut in Atlantic Canada, but somehow it managed. That program provided financial assistance to companies undertaking energy conservation, with a three to six-year pay-back period.
In addition, the Government has ended the Industrial Conversion Assistance Program, which helped industry to convert from oil to natural gas-fired boilers. Not only has it decided to cut the program, the Government has now said that it will pay only 50 per cent of the costs for those who have taken part in the program in good faith.
The Government does not care about people. All it cares about is the establishment. It wants to take money from Canadians-just like it is doing to our senior citizens-and give it to the multinational oil companies.
The Government has taken yet another service away from consumers. It has decided to end the Energuide labelling program. That provided consumers with energy consumption data for home appliances. The program did not cost the Government very much, but it helped consumers quite a lot. That does not seem to matter to the Government.

The agency says this country must start to conserve its energy sources. This is not going to happen with the introduction of such a Bill. This House cannot support a piece of legislation which does this to our country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few brief comments on third reading of
Bill C-24. The last time I spoke on this Bill, we were 15 days away from the implementation of one of the measures proposed in the Bill, namely the termination of the energy conservation program. As I said, the last time I spoke on this matter, it was about 15 days before COSP was to terminate, and CHIP was to terminate in about a year from then. I indicated that we in my riding felt particularly bad. I represent a riding in Ottawa which has some of the city's oldest housing stock. Although we have used these programs to better our housing stock and to conserve energy, we still have a lot of housing which requires attention and would have benefited from a government assistance program that encouraged insulation of our homes.

I would like first of all, Mr. Speaker, in the brief comments I have to make, to join all Hon. Members of this House in congratulating the Deputy Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, Mr. Paul Tellier, who was elected President of the International Energy Agency, based in Luxembourg, and to wish him the best success in his new role.
I regret that Canada ranks today, along with Luxembourg, as one of the countries which conserve the least and waste the most energy. This statement does not come from myself, it was made by the Agency in a recent report. I read in Le Droit newspaper dated June 17, and I quote: "The Agency- referring to the International Energy Agency-was critical of the Canadian government's decision to terminate the subsidy program for home insulation and to reduce the scope of the measures aimed at encouraging industries to conserve energy and to switch to alternate sources of energy".
Mr. Speaker, I think that at this point where we must take special care to preserve for the future generations the natural resources which we inherited, it is important that this Government should seriously consider the comments made by such an important body as the International Agency, set up in 1974 if my memory serves me right, for the purpose of advising and counselling member countries on matters of energy.
When he addressed the issue, the Minister told us that Canadians are aware of federal programs, of the need to conserve energy, of the benefits of insulation, of the benefits to be derived from better conservation. I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that some Canadians are aware of all that, but I would point out to the Government that in January 1985, we had here in Ottawa some 13,000 applications for natural gas, for converting from oil to gas, filed with companies, and of course they could not all be processed. Because of winter and bad weather conditions, the companies involved did not have

Mr. Speaker, what struck me during the second reading discussion of Bill C-24 was the near-unanimity on the value and benefits of those two programs. I do not think there was one Member, at least whom I heard, who condemned or criticized those two programs. Mr. Speaker, two speakers have mentioned the difference in selling price in Chicago. I guess they have persuaded me that perhaps they really do not understand the difference, and I would just like to put it into context.
If one went out to buy a case of apples and the apples were fresh and prime, they would cost more than a case of apples that were bruised or getting old. It is the same with crude oil. Some crude oil is a good barrel of crude oil which refines into such things as aviation fuel and gasoline for cars. That kind of barrel sells for a much higher price than a barrel of heavy crude which breaks down into, for instance, asphalt rather than aviation fuel. That is the difference in the price of a barrel of oil. It is very difficult. There are in the pricing market in Alberta something like 32 different types of barrels, each priced separately. If you start comparing, if you like, the bruised apples with the good apples, that is the kind of problem you are going to have with a price comparison. That is what it is called, an export charge on oil exported to the United States. It is a mechanism that is there to encourage exports of oil from

Canada to the United States. There are two charges. One is an export charge for exports and the other is a Canadian charge, both levied by the federal Government. I might say there is nothing that has been more maligned than the National Energy Program. A lot of myth has built up around it. The fact is that the National Energy Program wanted to make Canada self-sufficient by 1990. So did the Clark Government program in 1979. We are self-sufficient. This is June 1985. The reason we are self-sufficient is that we have had an economic downturn, we found more oil than we thought was available, we have practised conservation, but we are self-sufficient right now and that is something to be pleased about. We are also the most wasteful user of energy in the industrialized world, next to Luxembourg.
The National Energy Program wanted to have 50 per cent Canadian ownership. We have the most foreign-owned industry of any of the industrialized countries. Right now the figure is about 44 per cent Canadian-owned and about 56 per cent owned by countries abroad. That is still bad.
The National Energy Program erred in that it brought in PIP grants, these very rich grants that moved a lot of the exploration from the western sedimentary basin, and I hope some of the central Canadian Members will listen to this, out to the frontiers in the north. That hurt Alberta and Saskatchewan. The grants were ill-advised in the sense they were very wasteful. They totalled less than $8 billion. They helped some small Canadian companies to get into the major play so they
were successful there, but for $8 billion we could have bought Imperial Oil and had instant 50 per cent Canadianization.
The problem with the Petroleum Gas Revenue Tax was not that it was getting money from the oil industry. For the first time the oil industry was really paying taxes. That is what they did not like, that is what they hated, but there were some problems with the tax because it was like a provincial royalty. We western Canadians do not like the federal Government to have royalties because they are our resources, they belong to the provinces, although they are to be shared with the rest of Canada, under the Constitution. They are the vehicle of economic growth in western Canada if they are used properly. That is why we were critical of the PGRT.
What does this Government do? It attacks perhaps the most successful aspect of that National Energy Program, which was the conservation programs. They were working.
